meta.title: Who really said "Thought and theory must precede all salutary action; yet action is nobler in itself than either thought or theory"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Virginia Woolf. Anna Jameson printed it in 1854 as words Wordsworth said, and the popular version shortens her text. No Wordsworth writing has been found.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thought and theory must precede all salutary action; yet action is nobler in itself than either thought or theory'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Woolf: the line was printed in 1854, in Anna Jameson's Commonplace Book, as a remark by Wordsworth. Woolf was born in 1882.

answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — credited to Wordsworth by Anna Jameson
answer.authorDates: 1770–1850 · English Romantic poet (as reported by Anna Jameson)
answer.sourceLine: The earliest printing we found is Anna Jameson’s A Commonplace Book of Thoughts, Memories, and Fancies (London, 1854), where she gives it as something Wordsworth said: “Thought and theory,” said Wordsworth, “must precede all action that moves to salutary purposes. Yet action is nobler in itself than either thought or theory.” The popular wording shortens her text, and no Wordsworth poem, letter or essay containing it has been found.

source.heading: Where the line first appears

docMeta.dd: A Commonplace Book of Thoughts, Memories, and Fancies, Original and Selected
London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, 1854; 2nd ed., corrected, 1855
Part I, “Ethical Fragments,” no. 12 (p. 14 in the 1855 edition)

source.excerpt: “Thought and theory,” said Wordsworth, “must precede all action that moves to salutary purposes. Yet action is nobler in itself than either thought or theory.” Yes, and no. What we act has its consequences on earth. What we think, its consequences in heaven.
trail: 1854: Anna Jameson prints the remark in her Commonplace Book, crediting it to Wordsworth (1854 first edition, Internet Archive ↗).
1855: The “second edition, corrected” keeps the passage as no. 12 on p. 14 (1855 edition, p. 14 ↗).
Wikiquote lists the line in Woolf’s Misattributed section, saying it “appeared as early as 1854” in Jameson’s book, where it is credited to Wordsworth (Wikiquote: Virginia Woolf ↗).
Wikiquote’s Wordsworth page lists it as attributed to him by Jameson, citing p. 14 of the 1855 edition (Wikiquote: William Wordsworth ↗).
source.excerptNote: The first two sentences are what Jameson attributes to Wordsworth. “Yes, and no” begins her own reply, in which she argues that all worthwhile action must come from thought. The popular version trims “all action that moves to salutary purposes” down to “all salutary action.”

source.rightsNote: The source text is Anna Jameson’s Commonplace Book, first published in London in 1854, so it is in the public domain in the United States. The popular one-sentence version is an anonymous shortening of that 1854 text, not a new work by Woolf or anyone else we can name.

author.heading: Who it is actually credited to
author.bio: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, launched the Romantic movement in English literature with Lyrical Ballads (1798). This saying is credited to him only through Anna Jameson’s Commonplace Book (1854), which quotes it as something he “said.” It is a reported remark, not a line from any of his published works.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Woolf
misattribution.intro: Quote sites and social posts often credit this line to Virginia Woolf. The printed record shows it was in circulation as Wordsworth’s before Woolf was born.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it in Woolf’s Misattributed section and traces it to Jameson’s 1854 Commonplace Book (Wikiquote ↗). Woolf was born in 1882 (Wikipedia ↗), so she cannot have originated a line printed in 1854.

Jameson’s book is the only source for crediting Wordsworth. She introduces it with “said Wordsworth” and names no poem, letter or essay (Jameson, 1855, p. 14 ↗). Wikiquote’s Wordsworth page therefore lists it as attributed rather than sourced (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest printing found is Anna Jameson’s Commonplace Book (1854), which credits the remark to Wordsworth (1854 edition ↗). It is not Woolf’s, and her book is the only thing linking it to Wordsworth.

context.heading: A remark with a rebuttal attached
lead: The popular version leaves out that Jameson did not simply endorse the remark. Right after quoting Wordsworth, she replies “Yes, and no.” She then argues that what we do has consequences on earth and what we think has consequences in heaven, and that all action worth anything “must result from thought.”

Jameson’s Commonplace Book mixes her own reflections with things other people said. That is why this line has no standard source in Wordsworth’s collected works: in print, it exists only as her report.
context.pull: Yes, and no. What we act has its consequences on earth.
